newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa stocks seen at warehouse capacity.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa stocks seen at warehouse capacity.

text.p: Ivorian warehouses are swollen to capacity with cocoa following small December shipments, but levels will be cut marginally later this month, port sources told Reuters.
Ivory Coast's total cocoa warehousing capacity has never been disclosed officially but one port source said it was between 380,000 and 390,000 tonnes.

"You can count on 250,000 for Abidjan and about 80,000 to 90,000 for San Pedro," the source said. "The figure can change if other warehouses are opened but that is the usual dedicated space we deal with."

Total cocoa arrivals at the two main ports since October 1 stood at around 650,000 at January 13, sources said earlier this month. Export shipments totalled 10,000 tonnes in October, 131,000 in November, 122,000 in December and an estimated 100,000 tonnes for January, a port source said on Thursday.
"Some of January has yet to be shipped," said the source.
Arrivals figures since mid-January were not yet clear but sources said enough had been received to account for full warehouses.
"We are now somewhere over 700,000 tonnes," one estimated.
Exporters said stock levels were high partly due to prices bid on Ivory Coast's electronic auction system -- still unchanged in its first year despite industry demands for rule revisions.
"If the Caistab opens bidding at 770 (French francs per 100 kg) some companies are bidding as much as 800. That is beyond some of us," said one.
That could mean some exporters holding back tonnages to sell higher in later months with a better premium, he added. "March offers a 20 pounds premium so it would be in some of their interests."
Sources close to negotiations with the Caistab on the donor-sponsored implementation of auction rules told Reuters early changes were now unlikely.

"A European delegation visited at the end of December but there was no movement," said one source. "It will probably be left for the rest of the year (until 1997/98) so it has time to settle down into a pattern."
Two rule modifications had already been agreed by December by donor sponsors, including the World Bank and the European Union. Some differences with exporters remained, a source said.
Port stock levels are expected to drop before February.

"The stock levels are high but not extraordianary," said a shipping source, pointing to end-December levels which he put at 260,000 tonnes. Interest on loans and the possible loss of bean quality would have to be subtracted from price gains, if any.

Stocks in coming weeks were now dependent on trading currency movements, particularly in the French franc and sterling, along with mid-crop estimates due from this month after early up-country assessments, traders said.
Warehousing capacity was increased this year after one Ivorian firm, CAPA, converted an old beer factory warehouse for cocoa storage.

Some exporters also store more in inert-gased silos for bulk shipment and subsequent storage in the increasing number of dedicated European, and particularly Dutch, dedicated bulk reception facilities.
